youtube.title: Why Can't You Drive Through the Darien Gap?
youtube.description:
You can drive almost the whole way from Alaska to Argentina on the Pan-American Highway, except for about 100 kilometres of jungle and swamp between Panama and Colombia. Why has nobody ever closed the Darien Gap, and why did more than half a million people walk through it in 2023?

On the map we follow five centuries of plans that stalled here: the Spanish town of 1510, Scotland's lost colony, the 1924 border, the US-funded road stopped by a court in 1975, and the migrant route that changed everything. Then we look at three ways the gap could change, and what each would cost on the map.

{CHAPTERS}

sources.claim: The Pan-American Highway runs about 30,000 km from Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, to Ushuaia, Argentina
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pan-American Highway'; Guinness World Records, longest motorable road

sources.claim: The road ends at Yaviza, Panama, and resumes in northern Colombia near Turbo
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Darién'; Smithsonian Magazine coverage of the Darién Gap

sources.claim: Accounts of the gap's length differ, from about 97 km to 106 km
sources.source: National Geographic gives roughly 60 miles (about 97 km); other counts give 66 miles (106 km) from Yaviza

sources.claim: The Panama Canal opened in 1914
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Panama Canal' (opened 15 August 1914)

sources.claim: From Yaviza the way on is by boat on the Chucunaque River or on foot
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Darién'; Lonely Planet Panama guide, Darién section

sources.claim: Cerro Tacarcuna, on the Panama-Colombia border ridge, rises to about 1,875 metres
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Serranía del Darién'

sources.claim: The Atrato River ends in a delta of swamps and marshes on the Gulf of Urabá
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Atrato River'

sources.claim: Chocó is one of the rainiest regions on Earth
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chocó'; IDEAM Colombia rainfall records

sources.claim: Darién National Park (1981) and Los Katíos National Park (1994) are UNESCO World Heritage Sites
sources.source: UNESCO World Heritage List, sites 159 and 711

sources.claim: Darién National Park covers about 5,750 square kilometres
sources.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Darién National Park (575,000 ha)

sources.claim: Brunei covers about 5,765 square kilometres
sources.source: CIA World Factbook, Brunei

sources.claim: Emberá, Wounaan and Guna communities live in the Darién
sources.source: UNESCO site description; Government of Panama, comarca laws

sources.claim: The Guna govern their own semi-autonomous territory, Guna Yala
sources.source: Panama Law 16 of 1953 establishing the comarca

sources.claim: Travellers ship vehicles by container between Colón and Cartagena
sources.source: Lonely Planet Panama guide, overland travel section

sources.claim: Santa María la Antigua del Darién was founded in 1510 and abandoned by 1524
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Santa María la Antigua del Darién'

sources.claim: Balboa crossed the isthmus in 1513 with Indigenous guides and saw the Pacific that September, the first European known to see it from the Americas
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vasco Núñez de Balboa'

sources.claim: Panama City was founded in 1519
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Panama City'

sources.claim: Silver and gold crossed the isthmus on the Camino Real between Panama City and Portobelo
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Panama: Colonial period'

sources.claim: In 1698 about 1,200 Scots sailed to found New Caledonia
sources.source: National Records of Scotland, Darien scheme records; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Darien scheme'

sources.claim: Within a year hundreds of the first settlers had died and the colony was abandoned in 1699
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Darien scheme'

sources.claim: About £400,000 was pledged; estimates of its share of Scotland's money range from a fifth to a quarter
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Darien scheme'; Douglas Watt, 'The Price of Scotland' (2007)

sources.claim: Spain besieged the second colony and it surrendered in 1700
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Darien scheme'

sources.claim: Scotland and England merged into one kingdom in 1707; many historians see the Darien loss as one reason
sources.source: Union with England Act 1707, Article I; Douglas Watt, 'The Price of Scotland' (2007)

sources.claim: Panama separated from Colombia in November 1903 with US support
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Panama: Independence'

sources.claim: In 1923, at Santiago, Chile, the American states agreed to plan the highway
sources.source: Fifth International Conference of American States, Santiago, 1923; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pan-American Highway'

sources.claim: The 1924 Victoria-Vélez treaty fixed the border; it is 339 km long
sources.source: Treaty of Victoria-Vélez, 20 August 1924; CIA World Factbook, Panama

sources.claim: In the early 1970s the US agreed to pay two-thirds of the Darién section
sources.source: Sierra Club v. Coleman, US District Court for D.C., 1975

sources.claim: In 1972 a British expedition took two Range Rovers through the gap
sources.source: British Trans-Americas Expedition 1972; John Blashford-Snell's published accounts

sources.claim: In 1975 environmental groups sued and a judge halted the work
sources.source: Sierra Club v. Coleman, 405 F. Supp. 53 (D.D.C. 1975)

sources.claim: Foot-and-mouth disease was a concern; North and Central America are free of it
sources.source: Sierra Club v. Coleman (1975); USDA APHIS and COPFA (Panama-US Commission for the Prevention of FMD)
Panama National Migration Service, annual Darién figures (2021: 133,726; 2022: 248,284; 2023: 520,085; 2024: 302,203)

sources.claim: Most came from Venezuela, then Ecuador, Haiti and China
sources.source: Panama National Migration Service, 2023 by nationality

sources.claim: Many start in Necoclí, cross by boat to Acandí or Capurganá, then walk
sources.source: Human Rights Watch, 'This Hell Was My Only Option', 2023

sources.claim: Most take four to ten days
sources.source: Médecins Sans Frontières, Darién reports, 2023

sources.claim: More than 113,000 children crossed in 2023
sources.source: UNICEF press release, January 2024

sources.claim: The Gulf Clan controls routes on the Colombian side and charges fees
sources.source: Human Rights Watch, 'This Hell Was My Only Option', 2023

sources.claim: Walkers reach reception stations such as Lajas Blancas, then buses north
sources.source: UNHCR and IOM Panama situation updates, 2023-2024

sources.claim: In July 2024 Mulino signed a deal with the US for return flights; US to pay about $6 million
sources.source: US Department of Homeland Security statement and Reuters reports, 1 July 2024

sources.claim: Panama put barbed wire across several jungle paths
sources.source: Reuters and AP reports, July 2024

sources.claim: Panama's government said the wire was meant to close some paths
sources.source: Panama Ministry of Public Security statements, as reported by Reuters and AP, July 2024

sources.claim: US border policy hardened in early 2025
sources.source: US executive orders on border security, Federal Register, 20 January 2025

sources.claim: In early 2025 Panama reported crossings down more than 90 percent
sources.source: Panama Ministry of Public Security and National Migration Service statements, early 2025

sources.claim: In 2025 people moved south by boat along the Caribbean coast
sources.source: Panama National Migration Service and Reuters reports, 2025

sources.claim: Panama's government describes itself as a transit country
sources.source: Statements by President José Raúl Mulino, Reuters, 2024

sources.claim: Rights groups say closing paths pushes people onto hidden trails
sources.source: Human Rights Watch and MSF statements, 2024

sources.claim: Some officials and business groups in Colombia and Panama argue a road would carry goods and medicines overland at lower cost and bring services to river villages
sources.source: Smithsonian Magazine and Mongabay reporting on the Darién highway debate; Sierra Club v. Coleman (1975) record of the project's aims

sources.claim: Emberá and Guna leaders have said they fear a road would bring loggers, ranchers and settlers
sources.source: Smithsonian Magazine and Mongabay reporting on the Darién highway debate

sources.claim: Forest along the built road toward Yaviza became pasture
sources.source: Global Forest Watch tree-cover loss data, Darién province; Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute

sources.claim: A car ferry ran from Colón to Cartagena from 2014 and stopped about a year later
sources.source: Ferry Xpress service reports, 2014-2015

sources.claim: Some analysts warn the walkers could return if policies change
sources.source: Migration Policy Institute and IOM analyses of the 2025 Darién decline
